newsitem.title: USA: Little chance seen for U.S. budget deal this week.
newsitem.headline: Little chance seen for U.S. budget deal this week.

text.p: For all the talk of this being the "make-or-break" week for the White House and the Republican-led Congress to reach a budget deal, officials and analysts say there is only a slim chance of one by Friday.

And that chance appears to rest on conversations that are taking place outside of the formal budget talks on Capitol Hill between senior White House officials and the Republican chairmen of the congressional budget committees.

Administration and congressional officials said it was far from clear these informal talks would come to fruition by the end of the week and suggested that, in any case, they would at best produce an overall agreement without the detail needed for an accord on balancing the budget by 2002.
"There are a lot of conversations at a senior level above the level that is currently meeting," said one official who asked not to be identified.
"There are efforts to get there," said a second official. "They're trying, but I don't see it (happening)."

The idea of a Friday deadline has been pushed in public by Sen. Pete Domenici, the New Mexico Republican who chairs the Senate budget committee and who said on Sunday that this was the "make-it-or-break-it" week in the talks.

Domenici, a long-time budget hawk who wants to eliminate the deficit, also said that if the formal budget talks do not come to fruition this week, he would seek a budget agreement with Senate Republicans and moderate Democrats.
The deficit stood at $107 billion in fiscal 1996, which ended last September 30.

The formal Capitol Hill talks, now in their second week, include Domenici, House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich of Ohio, the budget committees' ranking Democratic members, and three top White House officials: Office of Management and Budget Director Franklin Raines, National Economic Council Chairman Gene Sperling and legislative director John Hilley.
Several analysts and officials, expressing what appears to be a majority view, suggested there was very little chance of an accord by Friday, which they described as a false deadline.

"The Friday deadline is completely phony," said Burson Marstellar budget analyst Stan Collender. "It's just the Republicans trying to put pressure on the White House and it's not working. A threat to go off and do your own budget would be credible if they had the votes, and they don't."
White House officials said they had pencilled in time on on Friday for President Bill Clinton to meet the Republican congressional leadership, should a meeting be warranted.
Such an occasion could be used to try to advance the budget talks if they are not making progress, or to bless any accords that had already been outlined by the staff.
Officials added that there was no certainty of any meeting actually occurring between the president and the congressional leaders, or even a lower-ranking group of the budget chairmen.

Asked if an agreement seemed possible by Friday, one official who declined to be identified said: "Not to me ... I would maintain there have been practically no negotiations so far. There have been discussions and background briefings, and all of that is necessary, but you still need much more."
The official was referring to the formal budget talks on Capitol Hill between the White House and the Republicans.

So far, there have been few signs of progress on the key issues that divide them -- the size of any tax cut as well as the cuts in the Medicare and Medicaid health care programmes, among others, needed to bring the budget into the black.
"People would consider it a major accomplishment if (by the end of the week) we have put ourselves on the forseeable path of getting there," said another official.
